Washington State.title: Washington State is changing a freshman's position, looking to bolster running back group | Notebook
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – For the final two games of the season, Washington State’s running back room will get a new member.

Freshman Lance McGee will transition from linebacker to running back for WSU’s last two games of the year, a road test against Texas State this weekend and the FLEX game, coach Kirby Moore said in his weekly news conference Monday.

Checking in at 6 feet and 218 pounds, McGee is listed as a linebacker and has repped at that position throughout practice this fall. But in the final moments of WSU’s blowout win over Colorado State over the weekend, McGee got one carry, signaling that coaches are ready to try him at the position where he excelled at last fall at Sumner High in the Seattle area.

“He’s had a unique path this first year,” Moore said of McGee.

Washington’s 4A state player of the year last fall, McGee rushed for 2,489 yards and 42 touchdowns, leading Sumner to a state championship. In the Spartans’ final two playoff games, McGee carded back-to-back 300-yard rushing outings, piling up 11 combined touchdowns in those two games alone.

He stole the show last season at running back, prompting Sumner coach Keith Ross to call McGee the best player he’s ever coached in a TV interview after the Spartans’ championship game win. But McGee began his high school career playing linebacker at A.C. Davis High School in Yakima, where he registered 115 tackles and six sacks as a junior, plus 868 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns.

Before transferring to Sumner, McGee caught the attention of several FBS schools on the West Coast and collected offers from WSU, Oregon State, Boise State, San Diego State, Colorado State, Nevada and Memphis. All those schools saw him as a linebacker, though.

McGee was originally committed to Oregon State, but he decommitted when former coach Trent Bray was fired and later flipped to WSU when Bray was hired as the Cougars’ new defensive coordinator.

Clemons, Pulalasi day-to-day

WSU wide receiver Darrius Clemons (ankle) and running back Leo Pulalasi (hip) are day-to-day with injuries, Moore said. Clemons was dressed and warmed up before WSU’s win over CSU, but he didn’t play, marking the third straight full game he’s missed. He sustained an ankle injury Oct. 9 against Utah State, then returned the following week against Oregon State, only to re-injure it in that game.

Clemons was “close” to playing, Moore said, but he didn’t wind up playing.

Meanwhile, Pulalasi exited early from Saturday’s game and returned to the sidelines in sweatpants and his uniform, out for the remainder of the game. On the year, he has totaled 34 carries for 140 yards and one touchdown, while the majority of the running back carries have gone to Kirby Vorhees and Maxwell Woods.

If Pulalasi misses time, it could open up an opportunity for McGee, who has yet to see the field as a true freshman. But a bowl game is out of the picture for the Cougars, and with traditional redshirt rules no more in favor of the 5-in-5 eligibility model, McGee could get on the field sooner than anticipated.

“Instead of waiting till spring ball and then there’s kinda no going back at that point,” Moore said, “we’re gonna determine that after the season what’s best moving forward for his career.”

Washington State.title: Fresh off historic offensive outing, WSU hits the road to take on surging Texas State | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against Texas State on Saturday evening.

What is it?

Coming off a historic 73-7 win over Colorado State, good for its first FBS win of the season and the end of a six-game slide, WSU hits the road to take on Texas State, which is tied for second place in the Pac-12. It’s the first meeting between the Cougars and Bobcats, the latter of whom was the last addition to the rebuilt conference last summer.

To reach the Pac-12 championship game, Texas State needs to beat WSU and get some help this weekend.

Where is it?

UCFU Stadium in San Marcos, Texas.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 3 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday morning, WSU was a 10.5-point underdog in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 73-7 win over Colorado State, WSU set all kinds of records. It was the Cougars’ highest point total in program history against an FBS opponent, and their first time hitting the 70-point mark since a 2024 win over FCS Portland State. They also totaled 535 rushing yards, the most in program history, aided by a 98-yard touchdown rush by running back Kirby Vorhees – the longest in program history and the longest in college football this season.

WSU scored touchdowns on just about every opportunity, including three from Vorhees and two from quarterback Owen Eshelman in the first half. In fact, the only times the Cougars didn’t find the end zone were when they didn’t have enough time: Before the buzzer on the first half, when kicker Jack Stevens hit a 33-yard field goal, and before the end of the game, when they took a knee to kill the clock.

It was a remarkable performance from the Cougars, who entered with one of the nation’s worst offenses, scoring only 18 points per game and rushing for just 124 yards per game. Those numbers skyrocketed against the Rams’ defense, which is on track to become the second-worst college football defense of all time, behind only the 2019 UMass group, which permitted 52.7 points per game.

Eshelman only needed to throw 14 passes, and he completed 13, for 135 yards and one touchdown, a 30-yard completion to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy in the third quarter. In his fourth career start, Eshelman added 13 carries for 81 yards and three scores, while tailback Maxwell Woods tallied 108 yards and one touchdown, his first since last year’s Potato Bowl.

But WSU’s top dog on Saturday was Vorhees, who piled up 197 rushing yards and four touchdowns, helping his team average a staggering 9.2 yards per play. His 98-yarder also tied for the longest in the history of the Pac-12, including the legacy and rebuilt versions. The Cougs averaged 9.2 yards per rush.

On defense, WSU also held Colorado State to a season-low seven points, and the Rams used two trick plays to score their one touchdown. The Cougars got an interception from safety Jaylen Thomas, his fourth of the season, and two sacks: one from reserve defensive end Michael Hughes, the first of his career, and one from cornerback Jalil Tucker, also the first of his career.

It was the first FBS win for the Cougs, who hadn’t won a game since a romp over FCS Duquesne in September.

Scouting Texas State…

Under fourth-year coach GJ Kinne and quarterback Brad Jackson, Texas State has won four of its last five games, its only loss in that span a wild road defeat to Boise State two weeks ago. The Bobcats are coming off a narrow home win over Fresno State.

Texas State has the Pac-12’s second-best offense, averaging a shade over 38 points per game, which is also No. 11 in the country. In his second year as a starter, Jackson has completed 197 of 285 passes (69%) for 2,502 yards and 22 touchdowns against only six interceptions. He’s also only taken 12 sacks, including just three in the last three games.

Jackson is also a dual-threat QB, averaging 5.2 yards per carry and seven scores on the ground. Also of note: WSU will be meeting former Cougar running back Jaylen Jenkins, who returns kickoffs for the Bobcats. He played the 2022 and 2023 seasons at WSU before being dismissed from the team early in the 2023 campaign.

Texas State’s offensive firepower also comes from veteran running back Torrance Burgess Jr., who has tallied 1,225 yards and six touchdowns on 178 carries, good for an average rush of nearly 7 yards. He’s cleared 100 yards in each of the Bobcats’ last two games, including a 196-yard effort against Oregon State and a 107-yard performance against Fresno State.

Texas State’s top targets are receivers Chris Dawn Jr. and Beau Sparks, who have combined to reel in 93 catches for 1,146 yards and nine touchdowns, forming a lethal threat down the field. The Bobcats also have a deep threat in sophomore Zechariah Sample, who has totaled 95 receiving yards in each of his last two games, including receptions of 47 and 43 yards.

On defense, the Bobcats are yielding 31 points per game, which is No. 6 in the conference. Most of their games have come in high-scoring affairs, including their last two outings, a 42-21 win over Oregon State and a 37-35 victory over Fresno State. But the Bobcats do tackle well, missing single-digit tackles in each of their past two games.

What happened last time?

This is the first meeting between WSU and Texas State.

Washington State.title: Boise State clinches as CFP expansion leaves future of conference championship in doubt | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

With its victory over Oregon State on Saturday evening, Boise State has secured home-field advantage in the first, and possibly last, championship game of the rebuilt Pac-12.

College Football Playoff expansion (to 24 teams) beginning next season has heaped doubt upon the competitive value and logistical feasibility of conference championships across the sport.

The ACC, Big 12, Big Ten and SEC announced last week that their title games will be eliminated in 2027, which makes perfect sense given that they are expected to have a barrage of participants in the expanded field.

But the American, Conference USA, MAC, Mountain West, Pac-12 and Sun Belt have a different calculation because they are essentially fighting for one spot in the 24-team field.

The Pac-12 has not determined its course of action.

“Because of our size, we have the option to continue it if we think it’s in our best interest,” commissioner Teresa Gould told the Hotline late last week. “Our North Star is always to get our champion into the CFP.”

There is no deadline for the Group of Six to inform the playoff of their plans for championship games next fall.

Gould views this season, in which the six leagues are competing for one playoff berth, as a window into best practices for the 24-team field.

“We want to get through this year and understand the criteria,” she said. “Is the 13th data point for our champion an advantage or disadvantage?”

The revised postseason calendar is one consideration. Under the current format, conference championships are staged on the first weekend of December; the Army-Navy game is the only competition on the second weekend; and the 12-team CFP begins on the third.

Next season, the opening round of the expanded CFP is slotted for the second week (Thursday through Saturday), which means Group of Six teams playing in their conference championships and advancing to the CFP would not have a break to heal and prepare for the playoff.

The only workaround: Moving the championship game to the final Saturday in November (i.e., rivalry weekend). That seemingly would be an option for the Pac-12, which has flexibility because of its size (eight teams).

“We would consult closely with CBS,” Gould said of the network that owns the rights to the Pac-12 championship. “The game is an important brand for us. It has a big impact on our business agreements.”

Like so much else about the 2027 season, including the bowl partnerships, the fate of the Pac-12 championship will play out over the next few months.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (9-1/6-0)

Result: beat Oregon State 46-41

Next up: vs. San Diego State (6:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: It doesn’t get much better than hosting ESPN’s ‘College GameDay’, winning a high-profile game, clinching home field for the conference championship and having one of your chief competitors for the College Football Playoff (New Mexico) lose at home – all in the span of 14 hours. (Last week: 1)

2. Texas State (6-4/4-2)

Result: beat Fresno State 37-35

Next up: vs. Washington State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: High likelihood that the Bobcats advance to the Pac-12 title game in Boise, the site of their one-point loss on Halloween. They need a victory over the Cougars and a San Diego State loss to Boise State. (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (5-5/2-4)

Result: lost at Texas State 37-35

Next up: vs. Colorado State (4:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The Bulldogs’ four conference losses have come by a combined 19 points, with two by a total of five. Flip the Texas State and San Diego State defeats, and the Bulldogs would be comfortably positioned for the conference championship game. (Last week: 3)

4. Oregon State (5-5/3-3)

Result: lost at Boise State 46-41

Next up: vs. Utah State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: The five-game winning streak that captured so much attention is crammed between a two-game losing streak and a three-game losing streak. As a result, the Beavers are in must-win mode (i.e., one of their final two) in order to secure a bowl berth. (Last week: 4)

5. San Diego State (5-5/4-2)

Result: beat Utah State 30-13

Next up: at Boise State (6:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: After all the injuries and illnesses and blowout losses and close wins and wobbly quarterback play, the Aztecs are sitting in second place, one step from the postseason. It’s quite the low-key impressive coaching job by Sean Lewis. (Last week: 6)

6. Utah State (4-6/3-3)

Result: lost at San Diego State 30-13

Next up: at Oregon State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: The Aggies are scheduled to host Boise State on Flex Saturday (Nov. 28), which would be a dangerous assignment for the playoff hopeful. But the Pac-12 would have limited options for sending the Broncos elsewhere because, per policy, they cannot return to Colorado State. (Last week: 5)

7. Washington State (2-8/1-5)

Result: beat Colorado State 73-7

Next up: at Texas State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: The Cougars scored 171 points in nine games (while losing eight of them) and then slapped Colorado State around for 73. The Rams are beyond bad on defense. But we have never, ever … ever … seen a script flip quite like that. (Last week: 8)

8. Colorado State (3-7/1-5)

Result: lost at Washington State 73-7

Next up: at Fresno State (4:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The Rams are allowing 47.6 points per game. Best we can tell, that is the worst scoring defense in major college football this decade. And there’s still time to hit 50! (Last week: 7)

Washington State.title: 3 thoughts from WSU's 73-7 win over Colorado State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Even as his first season at Washington State approaches its end, coach Kirby Moore has always been reticent to crack a smile in public settings. He has maintained something of a vanilla approach, at least when he’s addressing the media, regardless of the situation at hand.

In fairness, before WSU’s 73-7 win over Colorado State on Saturday, Moore didn’t exactly have many opportunities to beam. For six straight weeks, all he had to discuss were losses, reasons why his team’s offense was languishing and explanations why his team couldn’t string together enough winning plays. Moore could only say the same thing so many different ways.

Which is why one moment after Saturday’s game stuck out like a dab of crimson on a white cloth.

Moore was talking about his angle on running back Kirby Vorhees’ 98-yard touchdown rush, the longest in WSU program history and the longest in college football this fall. Then he began to smile.

“If I was gonna be honest, and I know he’s not in the room here, I was a little worried there at about the 45 ,” Moore said, “but he ended up opening it up, and I was kinda getting ready and flipping for the next call.”

Moore laughed. So did the room. If that doesn’t capture the vibes coloring the Cougars’ win, their first over an FBS opponent this season, who knows what does? They needed something positive to build on, anything at all, and the remedy was a Ram defense that is now allowing 47 points per game. If that number holds to the end of the season, it would be the worst since 2019 UMass, which gave up 52.7 points per game – the worst mark of all time.

So while that’s the kind of defense this WSU offense needed to face to pull off such a historic scoring outing, setting a program record for most points in an FBS game, there are other things to glean from this game. Here are three of them.

1. Don’t let the Cougars’ defensive showing fly under the radar

The headlines from this game will revolve around Colorado State’s defense, and rightfully so, given the Rams’ unit might be worse than the top FCS outfits. But in Saturday’s game, the other defense acquitted itself mighty well.

WSU’s defense came a couple trick plays away from pitching a shutout, which would have been the Cougars’ first time doing so since 2018. In fact, they checked off two boxes they have struggled to this season: They produced sacks and a turnover.

The Cougs engineered two sacks, one from cornerback Jalil Tucker and one from reserve defensive end Michael Hughes, who picked up the first of his career. It’s a nice accomplishment for Hughes, who is in his fourth year with the program, waiting the better part of three years to earn a consistent role. “I’m so happy for Mike, especially with dealing with injuries and stuff like that throughout his time,” linebacker Keith Brown said, “and he’s also matured a lot as a player.”

Plus, the Cougs forced one turnover, an interception from safety Jaylen Thomas. That’s his fourth of the season, which is the most by a WSU defender since former cornerback Ethan O’Connor reached the same mark two seasons ago. In fact, in the last six seasons, those are the only two WSU defenders to accomplish the feat.

It matters for a WSU defense that had struggled to generate sacks and turnovers. Entering Saturday’s game, the Cougars had forced only six turnovers, which was tied for No. 132 of 138 FBS teams. They also had gotten home for just eight sacks, which ranked No. 134. As the walls closed in on their season, it was becoming clear that their defense would need to improve on both fronts.

Plus, WSU didn’t just do so against a lowly offense. The Cougars accomplished that against a Colorado State offense that ranks among the Pac-12’s top half, including scoring point totals of 38 against Boise State, 56 against San Diego State and 27 against Texas State. The Cougars should be proud of their defensive performance, and defensive coordinator Trent Bray deserves credit for making sure Saturday’s game didn’t turn into a shootout.

2. Jack Stevens continues his impressive turnaround

It wasn’t long ago that kicker Jack Stevens was perhaps the most reviled member of WSU’s entire team, opening the season 1-for-5 on field goals. Not all of those were his fault – a couple were blocked – but the blame went to Stevens, whose shakiness was such a factor that it threatened to force the Cougars’ ineffective offense to be more aggressive in plus territory.

All of a sudden, Stevens has made 9 of his last 10 field goal tries. He has now connected on 10 of 16 field goals on the season. His only recent miss came on Halloween night, when he was asked to make a 53-yarder in the rain at San Diego State. Otherwise, he has been perfect since late September.

It’s easy to overlook his turnaround, especially since WSU’s offense has been to blame for this rotten season, but Stevens deserves his flowers. He took a beating online and in person. He had to put in lots of extra work to fine-tune his technique. In the face of what likely felt like daunting pressure, Stevens has recovered sharply, even nailing a pair of career-long 50-yarders.

3. A moment for WSU’s offensive line

Speaking of reviled characters on WSU’s team, five of the bigger ones play on the offensive line, one of this team’s top weaknesses this season. Across the Cougars’ first eight games of the season, it became clear that those five – left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell – had an outsize role in the Cougs’ languishing offense.

That remains true, but it’s also true that in their last two games, those five have looked much better. In that SDSU game, WSU’s front five earned a Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of 85.2, by far its best of the season, allowing just one sack on seven pressures. And on Saturday night against CSU, they earned a season-best run-blocking grade of 76.7, clearing the way for the Cougs’ sparkling night on offense.

Check out how those five graded out from Saturday’s game in the run-blocking department: Dunham was at 78.6, Caldwell was at 71.8, Bakken was at 77.4, Tripp was at 64.3 and Lester was at 59.9. That’s three above-average grades and two middle-of-the-road marks. Maybe those don’t blow you away, but they represent meaningful improvement for this group.

Did it help that the Cougars were facing a historically bad defense? Of course. We can’t emphasize enough how lowly this CSU defense is. In all likelihood, a lot of time will pass before college football sees a worse defense take shape.

But you have to play who’s in front of you, and WSU treated this CSU defense accordingly, dinging the Rams for their worst night of the season. The Cougars’ offensive line deserves a good helping of credit for paving the way.

Washington State.title: In breakthrough blowout, Washington State piles up records against Colorado State | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Back in August, after a sweltering afternoon practice, Kirby Moore strode up to a microphone and smiled. The young man who would go on to take over quarterback duties for Washington State, redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, had just tossed one of the prettiest balls of camp.

Moments prior, Eshelman had delivered the touchdown pass, a bomb downfield to Tony Freeman. At that point in fall camp, the Cougars’ offense was enjoying a scintillating day, especially from Eshelman, who was flashing his potential.

“When the stage presents itself,” Moore said, “we’ve gotta throw it.”

Sharp as his offense looked on that day, Moore probably could not have predicted it would roar to life the way it did three months later on Saturday night at Gesa Field, the site of WSU’s 73-7 win over Colorado State. The Cougars totaled a staggering 674 total yards and scored on their first 11 drives, torching a Ram defense that ranks as the nation’s worst.

In the Cougars’ top scoring outing against an FBS opponent in program history, they totaled 535 rushing yards, the program’s most in a single game. That included 197 and four scores from tailback Kirby Vorhees, including a program-record 98-yarder in the first half. Maxwell Woods also broke free for 108 yards and one touchdown, his first since last year’s Potato Bowl, while quarterback Owen Eshelman completed 13 of 14 passes for 135 yards and one touchdown – plus 81 yards and three scores on the ground.

Thanks to a late 60-yard rushing touchdown from quarterback Julian Dugger, the Cougars cleared 70 points for the first time since 2024, when they dropped 70 on FCS Portland State. But WSU had never hit the 70-point mark against an FBS opponent until Saturday night.

The points never quite stopped coming from the Cougars, who took a 38-7 lead into halftime, when kicker Jack Stevens connected on a field goal at the buzzer. That was the only time Moore’s team didn’t score a touchdown — when it ran out of time.

It was the kind of night that you don’t see often in college football. WSU’s 535 total rushing yards are the program’s most in a game ever, shattering previous records set in recent years. As part of that effort, the Cougs also got 46 yards from freshman Tre Hill Jr. and and 16 from Leo Pulalasi, whose night ended early. He wound up wearing sweatpants on the sideline for unclear reasons.

The Cougars scored 35 unanswered points to start the game, including the following: A 3-yard rush from Vorhees, a 98-yard rush from Vorhees, a 4-yard rush from Eshelman, a 9-yard rush from Eshelman and a 14-yard rush from Vorhees. His 98-yard rush earned several superlatives, including the longest rush in WSU program history, the longest in the country this season, and it tied for the longest rush in Pac-12 history — the rebuilt or traditional version.

In the second half, the Cougs continued to pour it on, scoring on a 30-yard touchdown pass from Eshelman to Branden Ganashamoorthy, who was open for too long, long enough for the Ram defense to catch him. But they had no luck in that department, watching Ganashamoorthy haul it in in the back of the end zone.

After that, it was still all WSU, which got a one-yard rush from Eshelman, a 10-yard rush from Vorhees and a 2-yard rush from Woods. That was before Dugger came on in relief and strode into the open field, jetting 60 yards into the end zone.

It was exactly the kind of night WSU’s offense needed, following nine games devoid of any consistent offense, even when they swapped quarterback Caden Pinnick for Eshelman. The Cougars’ rushing offense had never seen this kind of success. Entering Saturday’s game, their top three running backs were averaging 46 yards on 15 carries per game, underscoring how unheard of this outing was for these Cougars.

On defense, WSU permitted one Colorado State touchdown, a short rushing score late in the first half. But otherwise, it was more dominance from the Cougs, who also got an interception from safety Jaylen Thomas. It was Thomas’ fourth on the season, the most by a Cougar defender since Ethan O’Connor also nabbed four in 2024.

WSU returns to action next week, traveling to face Texas State on the road.

BOX SCORE

Key moments

WSU breaks single-game rushing record

4th, 1:50 – WSU 73, CSU 7: WSU’s Tank Hawkins cut outside and picked up 15 yards on the final play before the Cougars knelt out the rest of the clock.

That run put WSU at 535 rushing yards on the night – the new program record for single-game rushing, surpassing 524 yards in a 1984 win at Oregon.

The Cougars averaged 9.2 yards per carry and scored nine rushing touchdowns during their historic night.

Backup QB shows speed

4th, 9:10 – WSU 73, CSU 7: Backup quarterback Julian Dugger found an open lane on a keeper and raced 60 yards for a touchdown, the Cougs’ ninth TD run of the game.

The Cougs’ 73 points are their fifth-most in a game in program history, and most ever in a game against an FBS opponent. Their rushing output (481 yards) ranks second in WSU history for yards on the ground in a game.

Woods joins the scoring fun

4th, 12:13 – WSU 66, CSU 7: Maxwell Woods scored his first rushing touchdown of the game – the Cougs’ eighth TD on the ground, which ranks second in program history for rushing TDs in a game.

Woods has been involved otherwise, with 108 yards on 15 carries. The Cougs are up to 416 rushing yards – the sixth-most in a game for WSU in program history and the most since 1985.

Thomas snags his fourth pick

3rd, 1:39 – WSU 59, CSU 7: WSU safety Jaylen Thomas recorded his fourth interception of the season, reaching out for a nice grab on a toss from Hauss Hejny, who was trying to force a pass deep. The Cougars offense takes over near midfield.

Vorhees’ historic night continues

3rd, 3:48 – WSU 59, CSU 7: Running back Kirby Vorhees added another highlight to his career night – one of the best rushing performances in program history. He showed balance after being tripped up and dove over the goal line for his fourth touchdown of the game, this one a 10-yarder.

Vorhees is now tied for second in the WSU record books for rushing TDs in a game. He’s up to 197 yards on 12 carries, an average of 16.4 yards per attempt. He’s pacing a WSU ground game that has 380 yards and seven touchdowns.

Hung off edge on fourth-and-short run stop to force another TO on downs. CSU offense had been one of the most productive in the FBS, but it’s been outmatched by the Cougars defense tonight.

WSU keeps piling on

3rd, 7:14 – WSU 52, CSU 7: Quarterback Owen Eshelman continued his stellar day with his third rushing touchdown, faking a pitch and scooting in from 1 yard out. The redshirt freshman has four total touchdowns. He’s rushed for 68 yards and passed for 128 on an 11-for-12 completion rate.

The Cougars have surpassed their season high in rushing with 348 yards. They’re letting out their frustrations on the Rams. Their offense has been unstoppable – they’ve scored on all eight possessions – and they don’t seem to be slowing down.

That 56-yard scoring drive was set up by a turnover on downs. Jalil Tucker came unblocked on a blitz for a second-down sack. CSU elected to go for it on fourth-and-long near midfield, and the Cougars didn’t give up much on a short pass.

Coug passing game gets involved

3rd, 13:26 – WSU 45, CSU 7: WSU’s ground game had done all the scoring damage in the first half. The Cougars went through the air for their first touchdown of the second half. Quarterback Owen Eshelman faked a handoff and CSU’s defense – unsurprisingly playing the run – bit on the play action, and Eshelman fired deep to Branden Ganashamoorthy, who was left wide open for a 30-yard touchdown. Eshelman is now 11 of 12 for 128 yards with one passing TD and two scores on the ground.

WSU in control at halftime

Halftime – WSU 38, CSU 7: Cougs kicker Jack Stevens connected on a 33-yard field goal as time expired to complete an impressive scoring drive in the final 38 seconds of the first half.

The Cougs amassed 367 yards in the first half against 199 for the Rams. WSU has rushed for 300 yards, just 17 away from breaking the season high, set during a rout of FCS Duquesne. The Cougars’ maligned offense is humming against the nation’s bottom defense. It’s easily the best overall showing for WSU this year.

Running back Kirby Vorhees, who entered the day with 297 rushing yards for the season, has 158 yards and three touchdowns on the ground, including a 98-yard TD – the longest run in program history and the longest in the nation this season. Quarterback Owen Eshelman has rushed for 64 yards and two TDs, and completed 9 of 10 passes for 67 yards.

Rams get on the board

2nd, :38 – WSU 35, CSU 7: The CSU offense, which entered the game as one of the highest-scoring units nationally, had been held in check throughout the first half, but the Rams showed flashes of their usual selves during a quick scoring drive that ended with RJ Vick’s 1-yard touchdown run on a reverse.

Vorhees scores again

2nd, 2:16 – WSU 35, CSU 0: Cougs running back Kirby Vorhees plowed through a couple of Rams defenders for a 14-yard touchdown run, his third of the night. The scoring drive was set up by a third-down sack from WSU’s Michael Hughes to end CSU’s drive, then Jaylen Thomas returned the punt 39 yards to put the Cougars in good field position. WSU already has 322 total yards, surpassing its per-game average of 307 yards for the season. The Cougars have also surpassed their season high in scoring against FBS competition.

Eshelman rushes for another TD, Cougars dominating

2nd, 7:31 – WSU 28, CSU 0: After forcing a quick three-and-out, WSU marched downfield with ease again. Maxwell Woods and Kirby Vorhees broke off big runs to set up QB Owen Eshelman’s second TD run, a 9-yard burst to the outside. WSU is up to 255 yards on the ground.

WSU opens big lead

2nd, 12:27 – WSU 21, CSU 0: WSU capitalized on the takeaway. Quarterback Owen Eshelman took a keeper and stretched across the goal line for a 4-yard touchdown run. The redshirt freshman QB already has 46 rushing yards, and the Cougars have piled up 197 rushing yards – a season-high against FBS opponents – and three TDs on the ground, two from Kirby Vorhees.

Cougars get a quick takeaway

1st, :46 – WSU 14, CSU 0: Everything’s going right for the Cougars. Right after Vorhees’ long TD run, Rams quarterback Hauss Hejny tosses an errant pitch that bounced off the CSU tailback’s facemask. WSU defensive end Matyus McLain dove into a scrum to recover the fumble, setting the Cougars up inside the red zone.

Vorhees breaks free for record-breaking run

1st, :55 – WSU 14, CSU 0: On the very next play after WSU’s goal-line stand, running back Kirby Vorhees found a wide gap in the middle, made a defender miss with a juke, and burst into open field for a 98-yard touchdown run – the longest run in program history, the longest in the nation this season and tied for longest in Pac-12 history, according to WSU’s sports information.

WSU makes fourth-down stand

1st, 1:09 – WSU 7, CSU 0: The Rams got inside the Cougars 10-yard line with a 35-yard pass to RJ Vick, but WSU’s defense stood tall after that. On fourth-and-goal at the Cougs 2-yard line, WSU’s defense swarmed to force a turnover on downs with a stop at the line of scrimmage on a Durell Robinson run up the middle. 

WSU cruises downfield for touchdown

1st, 6:36 – WSU 7, CSU 0: Cougars running back Kirby Vorhees powers in for a 3-yard touchdown rush to open the scoring. It was one of the Cougars’ best drives of the season, especially on the ground, picking up several chunk gains against a susceptible Colorado State defense. Quarterback Owen Eshelman rushed for 30 yards and three running backs tallied 26 yards. Eshelman only threw one pass on the possession, a 12-yard completion to Branden Ganashamoorthy.

Cougs start game with a stop

1st, 12:10 – WSU 0, CSU 0: The Cougs give up one first down, but make a second-down run stop and force a short completion with a blitz to end Colorado State’s first possession. Promising start for WSU’s defense against an explosive offense.

Pregame

Washington State’s offense ranks among the least productive in the nation. Colorado State’s defense sits dead last in the FBS in points and yards allowed.

Something has to give Saturday night when the Cougars host the Rams at Gesa Field in Pullman for a Pac-12 matchup. Kickoff is set for 7:45 p.m. on CBS Sports Network.

WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12 Conference) is still winless against FBS competition under first-year coach Kirby Moore and the team’s scuffling offense has shouldered most of the blame, but the Cougs should have an opportunity to move the ball with better consistency against a porous Rams defense that allows 542.2 total yards and 44.8 points per game.

But nothing’s guaranteed with this WSU offense, which couldn’t sustain much rhythm in the Cougs’ last game, a 26-20 loss to a San Diego State team that also has one of the worst defenses in the FBS. WSU ranks No. 130 out of 138 FBS teams in both scoring offense (19 points per game) and total offense (307.1 yards per game).

WSU’s defense has been decent this year, but has dealt with some tackling slips in recent games, and has struggled to get home for sacks and force turnovers. The unit will be tested by a Rams offense that ranks 20th nationally in points per game (35.8) and 24th in yards (444.1). Colorado State put up 56 points and 549 yards in a win over San Diego State on Oct. 24, a week before the Aztecs held WSU to 20 points and 367 yards.

Still, this is probably WSU’s best remaining opportunity to get on the board in Pac-12 play. The Rams (3-6, 1-4), under first-year coach Jim Mora, have lost six of their last seven games, giving up 64 points last weekend in a loss to Boise State. The Cougars are 8.5-point favorites, according to Vegas Insider.

CSU had its travel delayed a few hours Friday due to nationwide FAA groundings, and conducted a walk-through on the tarmac while awaiting the green light to take off. The Rams arrived in Pullman around 9 p.m. Friday, according to a post from CSU’s social media.

Clemons goes through warmups

WSU receiver Darrius Clemons, who hasn’t played since injuring his ankle Oct. 9 against Utah State, was fully suited up and participated in warmups, indicating that the senior Oregon State transfer will try to play.

If Clemons does play, he’ll provide a boost for the Cougs’ passing game. The 6-3, 217-pound wideout recorded 218 yards on 20 receptions in six games before sustaining the injury.

Series history

WSU is 3-1 all time against the Rams. Colorado State won the first meeting, rallying to beat the Cougars 48-45 in the 2013 New Mexico Bowl. WSU handled the Rams 20-3 last season in Fort Collins, Colorado.

Washington State.title: WSU earns first win of season with 123-87 romp over NAIA school Northwest
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – As Washington State limped into its next home game, a matchup with NAIA school Northwest on Saturday morning, coach David Riley wanted to see his Cougars accomplish a couple things.

One: Get a win.

Two: Protect the paint.

In a 123-87 victory, WSU checked both boxes, earning its first win of the season to move to 1-3 overall. The Cougars also held the Eagles to under 40% shooting from inside the arc, completing the second task they wanted to achieve.

It’s the end of the three-game losing streak to open the season for the Cougars, who got a career-best 27 points from Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins and double-digit scoring outings from five other players, including 14 points from guard Lazerek Houston and 13 from wing Jaylen Harrell. They led by as many as 36, cruising the entire way.

“Just excited for us to get on the board, get a win,” said Riley, whose team lost 19 turnovers. “We’ve clearly got a lot of work to do as a team, and we’re still building our identity, but one big thing for us was making sure we protected the paint. That was something that really hurt us in the first three games, and I think we held them in the high 30s, somewhere around there from 2. And that’s something that we really focused on. A lot of points scored. It’s a team that presses and plays fast-paced. So excited for us to keep growing and getting better.”

WSU had few issues on offense, scoring the program’s most points since a 1991 victory over Alcorn State. The Cougars took advantage of serious talent and size advantages, scoring nearly at will wherever they liked. Guard RJ Jones and forward Tyler Kropp each scored 12 points, while big man Ladji Dembele added 11. Overall, the Cougs converted 68% of their shots from the field, including 37 of 43 from inside the arc – a sizzling 86%.

But for WSU, things didn’t go as swimmingly on defense, allowing the Eagles to connect on 14 of 41 triples (34%). Since 2015, Northwest has played 16 Division I teams. None of them have allowed the Eagles to score more points than the Cougars, who couldn’t keep the visitors from cashing in from deep.

Still, there’s context to think about. Northwest plays at a blistering pace, getting shots up quick and using a full-court press to ramp up the total possessions. The Eagles had 86 possessions, which is more than all the fastest teams in the country are averaging, which top out at 85.

But the Eagles also managed just 0.98 points per possession, a metric that evens out statistics and removes pace from the equation.

Which brings two realities to the surface: Northwest scored 87 points, a total WSU should have no business permitting against an NAIA team that entered 1-2 overall. But the Eagles play at a pace that few other teams do.

“Overall, it’s kind of a skewed deal,” Riley said. “Our big thing was, we’re gonna make sure we protect the paint. That’s been our Achilles heel so far this season. So we gotta do a better job with that. There’s still some areas I thought when we got tired, and after the first couple minutes, we were still spread apart.

“That’s something that we need to continue to grow. … There’s five or six games a year where you might lose from 3, if you don’t guard the 3-point line well. A lot of the time it’s from 2. We gotta do a better job guarding the ball in transition, in the post, and really just having more drama at the rim.”

“We just gotta talk more,” Akins added. “That’s definitely concerning for sure. We gotta be better on that end.”

Another factor in this game: WSU played without transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who missed his third game with an ankle injury. He missed the first two with the injury, then returned to action last week against Duquesne, only to re-injure it in the final five minutes of that contest.

On Saturday, Riley described Harrison’s status as day-to-day, saying, “Just trying to get him back healthy.”

WSU returns to action on Wednesday, taking on Hawaii in Everett. The Rainbow Warriors have opened the season 3-1.

Why Washington State will beat Colorado State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – After nearly two months of losses, six straight games ending in defeats, help is on the way for Washington State.

It comes in the form of Colorado State, which had a late departure Friday for the game, set for Saturday night. Thanks to a nationwide flight grounding, the Rams were delayed hours in the Fort Collins area in the chaos, which prevented a host of teams across the country from reaching their destinations.

Even without that development, we would pick the Cougars to down the Rams, who harbor the nation’s worst defense in a bevy of categories. But because of the travel issues, WSU might be in an even better spot as it seeks its first FBS win of the season, which we’re picking the Cougs to secure.

Here’s the type of defense WSU and quarterback Owen Eshelman are set to square off with. The Rams rank last in scoring defense (45 points per game), last in total defense (542 yards per game), second-to-last in third-down conversion defense (54%) and last in yards per play (8). They have permitted scoring outings of 41, 59, 56, 66, 49, 31 and 64. That’s a key reason why they’ve dropped six of their last seven games.

The Cougars have fared worse in the win/loss column, but the Rams’ defense might present the solution to their ailing offense, which couldn’t complete a comeback against San Diego State on Halloween night. Look for WSU’s rushing offense to look a tad better, which could open up things for Eshelman, which gets a Rams defense that is giving up 11 yards per pass – last in the country.

Final score: WSU 30, Colorado State 24

Washington State.title: Amid nationwide flight stoppage, WSU set to host Colorado State
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The night before Washington State was set to host Colorado State, the Rams got a little extra practice in.

In the chaos of the nationwide flight grounding that swept college football and threatened Saturday’s game between WSU and CSU, set for 7:30 p.m. in Pullman on CBS Sports Network, the Rams found themselves on the tarmac at the Northern Colorado Regional Airport. So they got out and did a walk-through outside the plane.

If nothing else, it captured the confusion that flooded the country on Friday, when the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to be grounded from early afternoon until around 6 p.m. Some teams had already arrived at their destinations safely. Others waited hours for delays. Still others pivoted and took buses.

Looking to earn its first FBS win of the year and end a six-game losing streak, WSU might hope the delays play to its favor. The Cougars (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) are seeking a win over the Rams (3-6, 1-4), who have lost six of their last seven games and harbor the nation’s worst defense in all kinds of categories.

In that way, it’s the biggest opportunity of the season for WSU, whose scuffling offense has been to blame for this wayward season. In his fourth career start, Cougar quarterback Owen Eshelman and his offense will look to take down a Colorado State defense that ranks like this nationwide: Last in scoring defense (45 points per game), last in total defense (542 yards per game), second-to-last in third-down conversion defense (54%) and last in yards per play (8).

Could that be the solution to the Cougars’ ailing offense, which is coming off a bye week? It’s certainly possible, and it might represent WSU’s best chance at an FBS win this fall. After this game, the Cougs will round out the season with a road matchup against Texas State, then a home FLEX game, which will likely bring Oregon State to Pullman for a second clash between the Beavers and Cougars.

Those two games don’t profile as clear-cut chances to earn wins. WSU’s home game against Colorado State does – especially considering the travel delays that the Rams faced getting into the area.

“You can’t let the results dictate your behavior,” WSU defensive tackle Kaden Beatty said at the beginning of the week. “It’s like Coach Moore says: same guy every single day. I love this. I love playing football. I’m on fire for my work every single day. I come in here with a smile, regardless of our record. If we have no wins or we’re winning every single game, I’m gonna be on fire for my work and excited to be in this building.”

The Cougs could use some of that mentality to take down the Rams, especially considering that starting wide receiver Darrius Clemons is questionable with an ankle injury, which he suffered last month against Utah State. He has missed the past three games. With 20 catches for 218 yards, his absence has made things even harder on a Cougar offense trying to find its footing.

What will that look like on Saturday evening? Here’s one possibility worth keeping an eye on: How will the Cougar running backs fare? As the team heads into Week 11, WSU’s trio of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi are averaging a meager 46 yards on 15 carries in nine games against FBS competition. They haven’t managed any consistency, but that could change against the Rams’ defense, which is permitting an average of 271 yards per game – dead last in the country by nearly 30 yards.

That could be a real boon for the Cougs’ rushing attack, which figured to be one of the team’s top strengths headed into the season, especially considering the time and effort coach Kirby Moore spent luring Vorhees and Pulalasi away from the transfer portal. They haven’t been able to deliver on that, and part of the blame goes to the WSU offensive line, which has often languished in the short-yardage department.

What’s the solution to those problems? There may not be an obvious long-term fix, but one of the short-term variety could be facing the Rams’ defense, which is averaging 6.8 yards per rush – also last in the country. Opponents are also averaging nearly 280 rushing yards per game against CSU, which fired previous defensive coordinator Tyson Summers mid-game against Oregon State earlier this year. That hasn’t done much to shore things up for Jim Mora’s team, which gives up about 11.4 yards per pass, another mark that ranks last in the country.

“It’s just another great opportunity for us to run the ball,” WSU left tackle Ashton Tripp said. “And then, like I said earlier, just getting back to the basics. Break their will and make them quit.”

Still, WSU shouldn’t view this as an easy win. For as rotten a season as the Rams’ defense has had, their team has some reasons for optimism. Their 10 sacks are better than WSU’s eight. And CSU ranks first in the Pac-12 in forced fumbles (eight) and interceptions (nine). That should be a warning for Eshelman, who threw an interception in his group’s last game, a road defeat to San Diego State on Halloween night.

Above all, though, WSU needs a win in this game. The Cougars could be looking at a one-win season without it. Can they deliver? Ironically, they may be getting some help from an unexpected source: air traffic delays.

Washington State.title: With flight stoppage lifted, Colorado State expects to take off late Friday for WSU game
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State’s opponent this weekend, Colorado State, expects to fly out late Friday for the contest.

After the Federal Aviation Administration lifted a nationwide flight stoppage on Friday afternoon, the Rams are scheduled to fly out Friday night from the Fort Collins area, according to a report from the Coloradoan. That followed an hourslong delay, which forced a host of teams around the country to tweak their travel schedules.

As of Friday evening, the Cougars and Rams remain scheduled to kick off at 7:30 p.m. Saturday on CBS Sports Network.

For much of Friday, flights in the United States were grounded until further notice, the Federal Aviation Administration announced Friday afternoon, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” The issue was caused by a temporary telecommunications outage, the FAA said.

There is no known threat to the country, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, but for most of the day, it remained unclear when flights would be cleared to resume. Lots of teams around the country were grounded, including Washington, Texas, UNLV, Auburn, Tennessee and others. But others had already arrived at their destinations, including Nebraska, Florida and Wake Forest.

WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) is looking to earn its first FBS win of the year and end a six-game skid with this home game against CSU (3-6, 1-4), which has dropped six of its last seven contests.

Washington State.title: Eleonora Villa's late flurry lifts Washington State women past Southern Utah
Washington State.summary:
From staff reports

PULLMAN – Eleonora Villa tallied 13 of her 23 points in the fourth quarter, including a few crucial buckets in the final moments, to lift the Washington State women’s basketball team to a 72-69 nonconference win over Southern Utah on Friday night at Beasley Coliseum.

Villa hit a 3-pointer with 2:38 left to cap a 7-0 Cougars run that tied the game. She knocked down another triple with 1:12 remaining to put WSU (2-2) ahead by two points. About 30 seconds later, the standout senior guard converted a layup while drawing a foul, then hit the free throw to put the Cougs up by five – enough to hold on against the pesky Thunderbirds (2-2), who led for over 21 minutes of the game and were up by three possessions on multiple occasions.

Guard Mackenzie Chatfield had 18 points and 10 rebounds for WSU. Forward Ava Uhrich led the T-birds with 19 points and 11 rebounds.

The teams had almost identical shooting numbers – 23 of 56 from the field, 5 of 18 on 3s and 21 of 25 from the line for WSU; 23 of 55 from the floor, 4 of 14 from long range and 19 of 25 from the foul line for SUU.

Washington State.title: From dogs in cowboy hats to starry nights, WSU DE Matyus McLain loves his new painting hobby
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The first time Matyus McLain sat down to try his new hobby, his mind wandered to his childhood, back when he would battle his younger brother in video games. Matyus and the younger Mason played all kinds of games, and they still do, but one they frequented the most was LEGO Star Wars.

So on this August day, before he kicked off his first season starring at defensive end for Washington State, McLain sat down at his kitchen table, cleared everything off, spun some tunes using Spotify DJ, got his supplies out and got started.

He dipped his paintbrush into yellow paint to paint two characters, into brown to illustrate a background, into red to draw a series of hearts representing health. He may not have been happy with the way the door to the rest of the game turned out – “my depth isn’t awesome,” he says – but after about an hour had passed, he had a final product.

“It’s a great escape because it allows you to relax,” McLain said, “and it’s not you scrolling on your phone, playing video games.”

Since the beginning of fall camp in the summer, McLain has picked up a new hobby: painting. He’s completed about seven pieces so far, he said, everything from the LEGO Star Wars lobby screen to a photo of his dog wearing a cowboy hat to a skyline view with a moon hanging in the distance. Throughout a long and taxing season, McLain has used his new pursuit to get away from the grind, to focus on a new challenge.

Each painting takes him about an hour to an hour and a half, he says, reflecting the care he takes with each work and his desire to keep improving on them. When he sits down at his kitchen table to paint, sometimes he doesn’t do so with a specific idea in mind. He goes with the flow. He knows he isn’t an expert, saying, “I’m not great at it by any means.” But for now, he’s OK with that.

For McLain, who didn’t grow up a particularly artsy kid, where did this come from? The answer isn’t as profound as it may seem. On an off day during the Cougars’ fall camp in August, he said, the idea just came to him. I’m gonna paint something, he remembers telling himself. So he went to Walmart, picked up a set of painting supplies, and painted the LEGO Star Wars scene.

Since then, he’s authored a few pieces of artwork. The painting of his dog Brutus, a black and tan Coonhound, came from a real photo with the pup wearing a cowboy hat. He painted a scene with a tree with a stream of water running underneath. He has another more abstract painting, and for that one, he tried to use duct tape to imprint a line – “but the duct tape didn’t really seal the lines perfect,” he laughed.

“I would, like, lay the duct tape down so that way, I could paint over it and then peel off the duct tape, and it’d be a straight line,” McLain said. “Didn’t go as I imagined.”

When he sits down to paint, McLain has a pretty simple workflow. He uses Apple Music for his tunes, but he wants more of a variety when he paints, and for that he turns to Spotify DJ. That program gives him all kinds of music, from middle school throwbacks to hit Juice WRLD songs. He’s even been hit with some ’60s music, which he isn’t normally into. “The DJ thinks I am,” he chuckled.

In truth, though, the idea didn’t appear in his head like Dom Cobb planted it in the movie “Inception.” He comes from an artistic family. His main inspiration is his great-aunt Robin Peterson, a WSU veterinary school grad in the class of 1980. She does some illustration work, and a few of her pieces hang on the walls of McLain’s apartment. Those helped push the idea into McLain’s head.

Besides, he was around lots of art growing up. McLain’s great grandfather, John Fister, was a carpenter who built a kid-sized picnic table that McLain used to color on as a kid. He also built boxes, chairs and coffee tables. He sold some. Others still live at the McLain residence in nearby Priest River, Idaho, and McLain grew up around those as well.

Matyus’ uncle, Denny McLain, is also a carpenter. And his grandfather on his dad’s side, Tom McLain, is a musician based out of Chewelah. He plays mainly bluegrass, but his repertoire includes far more. “He is a master musician,” said Matyus’ mom, Julianne.

“It plays into the mental fortitude that he has,” Julianne added. “I think that he has a significant amount of mental fortitude, and it’s only grown and developed throughout the years. And I think having space to do extra things … I know in the summertime, it’s often going outside, getting in the river, the lake, and going for a hike or whatever it is that he’s doing. I think this is a different way, because I think they decompress on video games quite a lot. These kids, they enjoy the social connection of video games, and so I think it’s a productive way to increase his mental fortitude.”

“That part doesn’t surprise me,” Peterson added. “He was always just such a happy kid, you know? Not wild and crazy or anything, but always interested, curious about things, and interested and game to do anything. I think his parents helped instill the confidence that it takes to do that kind of stuff and just to do what he’s doing now, and so we’re very proud of him.”

McLain picked up painting in large part to get away from football, to give himself a release that isn’t trying to push back offensive linemen and get home for a sack. That much he has accomplished, and to those who know him best, the process started years back.

When McLain was a junior at Priest River, his wrestling team was at the state tournament meet down in Pocatello. During one match, McLain was trying a move that took him some time to maneuver and get into place, and it took long enough that the referee called him for stalling. He went on to fall in the match. His parents could tell he was frustrated.

Sitting up in the stands, Julianne remembers thinking, What is he going to do? Matyus shook his opponent’s hand, then went to a corner of the Holt Arena dome and sat down for some 45 minutes. After that, he got up and strolled over to the referee. Later, he would relay that he asked the ref what he saw on the stalling sequence. What caused him to call that?

It was an encouraging sight for Julianne, who has always encouraged her children to sit with the frustrating emotions, not fight them. That’s what makes us human. Years later, McLain has experienced his fair share of them playing for the Cougars, who are looking for their first FBS win this weekend against Colorado State, looking to shake off a six-game slide.

“When he says nobody’s giving up – there’s nobody giving up,” Julianne said. “He’s got lots of really strong teammates with really high character around him, and they’re all supporting each other. And I think that’s very accurate of what’s happening. So he’s got a lot of support even in the midst of the frustration.”

When he’s painting, though, McLain feels none of that. It’s just him and the canvas – not his phone, not TV, not video games. He really wants to improve at painting, he said, a nod to the competitive nature that helped him ascend from Priest River to Idaho to Washington State.

“I think it’s just a fun challenge outside of football,” McLain said. “It’s not scrolling on my phone. I get to relax, listen to music, and try to be good at something.”

Washington State.title: Turnovers have often eluded WSU, which has forced only six. How can the Cougars turn that around?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – A steady pitter-patter of rain fell overhead, providing a melancholy soundtrack on top of the locker room at Snapdragon Stadium, the site of Washington State’s latest showing. Jaylen Thomas, the Cougars’ best safety, stood in front of a crimson-and-white backdrop, his white jersey sporting a black stain on his right shoulder and a mix of black and green near the center of his uniform.

It was Halloween night, and things had gotten spooky for the Cougars, who had just dropped a six-point decision to the Aztecs. They made things interesting late in the fourth quarter, scrapping within one score, but their comeback fizzled out with a turnover on downs. They fell to 1-8 with the setback.

Thomas, though, had done his part. He earned the biggest stains on his uniform early in the third quarter, when linebacker Keith Brown tipped a pass into the air, where Thomas reeled it in and returned it 17 yards before he was dragged down deep in SDSU territory. It was his third interception of the season, the most by a Cougar since 2024.

“Keith made his play, and I was just in the right spot at the right time,” Thomas said. “Happened to be under the ball. Trusted myself, and just let my athleticism take over after that.”

One of Thomas’ best attributes is his awareness. In his first season at WSU, he’s leveraged it all kinds of ways: To snare two interceptions against Kansas State, to return one of them for a touchdown. To take a punt back for a touchdown against FCS Duquesne the week after. To break up two other passes in the games since. “I feel like putting in the work now,” he said back in September, “so I can have an easier life later.”

But only moments after describing his interception against SDSU, he used his awareness in a different way. He used it to add this: “Gotta create more takeovers from a defensive standpoint to help the offense start in a better position on the field and just help the team overall, with the turnover battle as well.”

It was a cogent point from Thomas, whose group has struggled to force turnovers this season. In nine games, the Cougars have forced only six turnovers, which is tied for No. 132 of 138 FBS teams. Only two other teams in the country have created fewer. Ahead of WSU’s final stretch of three games, which begins with a home matchup against Colorado State this weekend, it’s becoming a blight on the Cougs’ resume.

Here are the five turnovers that WSU’s defense has forced: Thomas’ two interceptions against Kansas State, Jackquintin Bal’s pick-six against Arizona, a fumble forced by Jirah Leaupepetele and recovered by Khamari Terrell against Fresno State, plus Thomas’ interception against SDSU. The Cougars also get credit for Utah State’s muffed kickoff, which was recovered by linebacker Carsten Reynolds, but strictly speaking, that doesn’t belong to their defense.

With those turnovers, the Cougars have given themselves chances to swing games and eke out wins, but those have not surfaced for this group. Their defense has forced only one turnover in their last four games, and that may not be the whole story from WSU’s recent stretch of setbacks, but goes a decent way in explaining the reasons behind them.

Think about this, which Thomas also seemed to be aware of: The Cougars’ inability to generate turnovers is costing their offense, and even with redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman looking sharp at the controls, that unit has left something to be desired too. WSU currently ranks four spots up from dead last in BCF Toys’ field position rankings, checking in at No. 134 nationally.

Additionally, the Cougars have only started about 7% of drives past their own 40 yard line, which can be traced in large part to their defense’s lack of turnovers.

So what’s behind that pattern? One of the biggest explanations is one number: Eight. That’s WSU’s total sacks this fall, which ranks No. 134 in the country. Only two other teams have brought down opposing quarterbacks less. The Cougars have not registered any sacks in their last three games.

For WSU, it registers as something of a surprising development, especially considering the weapons that defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk have flourished into. McLain has picked up 25 QB pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, which ranks fifth in the Pac-12. But he’s only gotten home for one sack. Zunk has swarmed in for 18 pressures, but he has only two sacks to his name.

It raises the burning question: What gives?

“I think naturally, teams we play do have a plan to get the ball out,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said, “or they’re chipping Matyus and Linus, and so you gotta give them credit as well, and that’s forced them to get the ball out quicker at times. We’ve been close. We had opportunities even in the San Diego State game there, where the quarterback got out, kinda made a late lateral there to the back.”

“We gotta finish,” Moore added. “That’s definitely something that we looked at on the opportunities that we had as well, because a lot of times when you get a sack, it at times can equal a sack-fumble, and you create a turnover.”

Can the Cougars force one or two of those against Colorado State? The Rams may have the country’s worst defense, allowing an average of 45 points per game, but they actually rank No. 18 nationally in turnover margin: plus-6. They’ve lost only 8 turnovers, which is No. 24 in the country and second in the Pac-12.

To earn FBS win No. 1, WSU may have to turn that trend around. The good news for the Cougars is they have a guy who has become pretty skilled at being in the right place at the right time.

“It starts at practice, just taking everything more seriously,” Thomas said after the SDSU game. “Just looking, having some self-reflection and just looking inward. Everybody having the mindset of, ‘what can I do better to help the team?’ I really take that to heart. Try to just focus on what I can control to help the team succeed, and you that’s what we all try to do.”

Washington State.title: 'My mindset is switched': How WSU DT Kaden Beatty is guiding the Cougars through a situation he knows well
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Kaden Beatty remembers the dark days like they just vanished over the horizon. He was in his second and final year at Kent State, where things weren’t just bad. They were miserable.

Back in 2024, Beatty played nearly 400 snaps in six starts for the Golden Flashes, who slogged through loss after loss, blowout after blowout, making things interesting in only two of those setbacks. He got home for a sack against Ball State, which won by two. He surged in for a tackle for loss against Bowling Green, which won by three scores. No matter what he did, no matter how well he played, his team just kept losing.

So, Beatty remembers, he began to feel sorry for himself. His feet started to meander, his mind began to wonder. Can I just get to next season? he thought to himself. Am I gonna leave this place?

“That’s just not how it is here,” Beatty said.

Beatty was referring to this Washington State team, which finds itself in a similar position. The Cougars have won just one game this fall, a blowout win over an FCS club. Since mid-September, the Cougars have lost six straight games, struggling to find anything resembling consistency in coach Kirby Moore’s debut season. They’ve tried all manner of adjustments – Moore took over playcalling duties last month, then changed quarterbacks – and nothing has resulted in a win, going 1-8 overall.

Naturally, that puts the Cougars at risk of splintering in the same ways that those Golden Flashes did. Back then, Beatty remembers, “it was kinda clashing amongst the team, amongst the coaches.” Not the case here in Pullman, he says, explaining that these Cougs have a stronger sense of resolve and resiliency.

Much of that starts with Beatty, one of six captains on this WSU team. In his second season as a Cougar, he has emerged as one of the faces of the program, a vocal leader and a charismatic defensive lineman. During TV timeouts, he’s on the sideline dancing, urging the Gesa Field crowd to match his energy. After his best plays – he has 21 tackles, one for loss – he’s screaming to himself, celebrating with teammates.

If you could make a leader in a lab like you were creating a player in “Madden,” you would probably end up with someone like Beatty, who has used his compelling combination of leadership and physicality and likability to do his part in keeping this WSU team together. He plays a thankless position, often invisible in the chaos at the line of scrimmage, which makes his maturity even more remarkable.

In fact, at halftime of WSU’s win over FCS Duquesne, the Cougars were only up one score. According to defensive end Matyus McLain, the most motivation came from Beatty, whose Kent State team lost to FCS Saint Francis in that 2024 season.

“I met with Kaden during the bye week,” Moore said. “That is a guy who loves football, and so every day when we get the opportunity to go out there between the lines, he’s energizing his teammates. He’s energizing the staff. I think he’s playing at a high level, and so we gotta do that throughout these last three weeks.”

“He’s a great leader,” WSU running back Maxwell Woods said in September. “He’s really like the voice of the team. He’s a guy like you’ll never really know if he’s down, if he’s happy. He always kinda stays at that same energetic level.”

What’s interesting is this: Over the last two years, how has Beatty evolved in his approach to losing seasons? What did that take?

Back at Kent State, where he redshirted during the Golden Flashes’ one-win 2023 season and emerged as a key player during their winless 2024 campaign, he found himself focused on himself. “It was all about me, me, me,” he said. When he thought about the season, his mind drifted to himself: Why is this happening to me? Why am I in this situation?

“And that’s not what it is at all here. It’s bigger than me,” Beatty said. “I feel worse for these fans and worse for this place than I do myself because they’re really rooting for us. They’re getting behind us, and we’re not giving them the product that they want. Tears me apart. So all I can do is the next thing. All I can do is figure out – how can I be better for us? And so that’s all I’m focused on.”

Beatty is right that the Cougars aren’t giving fans the product that they want, and for the first six weeks of the season, his group wasn’t the one at fault. Those honors went to the Cougars’ offense, which failed to beat a single FBS team under quarterback Caden Pinnick, whose struggles made things exponentially difficult on not only his offense, but his team’s defense as well.

As a result, Moore benched Pinnick for redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, who has looked better than his predecessor in his three starts. But in the Cougars’ last two losses, a home setback to Boise State and a road defeat to San Diego State, their defense has begun to fall behind too.

The Cougars missed 10 tackles against the Aztecs and another 18 against the Broncos. They also didn’t register any sacks in those two games, keeping their season total at just eight. Only three other teams in the country have registered fewer. Beatty may not be an edge rusher, but he bears some of the blame in that department, totaling just one QB pressure in each of his last three outings apiece.

He’s well aware of that. In fact, that’s one reason why Beatty spent last week’s bye week watching tape from his team’s first nine games of the season, doing what he called “self-evaluation.” He examined his performance against the run and against the pass – “and what I could do, really, just my 1/11 on the team to excel and to really help us get these wins,” Beatty said.

How has he fared on that front? According to Pro Football Focus, Beatty has earned an overall defense grade of 55.4, which ranks last among the 13 defenders who have played at least 200 snaps. His run defense has given him a grade of 55.1, second-to-last among qualified defenders, and his pass rush has resulted in a figure of 57.3, the best mark among rotation defensive linemen.

Those numbers may not raise many eyebrows, but it’s also true that PFF grades aren’t perfect, and if you watch WSU games, you know that Beatty usually finds himself in the middle of the Cougars’ best run stops. He’s an irreplaceable part of this WSU defense. His snap count, 308, reflects as much.

He’s playing some of his best football. His team is not. He had something of a similar experience two years ago, and since then, Beatty says, “my mindset is switched.” After a loss earlier this year, he was nearly shaking when he expressed his resolve to be better: “Nobody is more pissed off than this team.”

Will that help WSU take down Colorado State this weekend and earn FBS win No. 1? Maybe. The only thing that’s clear is that Beatty will keep showing up, will keep energizing his teammates, will keep being the kind of leader that this Cougar team needs.

“We’re toughening our skin,” Beatty said. “We’re getting tough right now, and this football team needs it. What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, like I just said. Those little nicks, those losses, those cuts that we’re getting every single week, we’re gonna heal it, and we’re gonna get stronger from it. We’re gonna excel and be able to get over those obstacles and conquer those mountains.”

Washington State.title: 'This is unacceptable': WSU falls to Duquesne in final moments, 72-71, opening season with three straight losses
Washington State.summary:
Over the weekend, after his Washington State group dropped a close road loss, David Riley went on the radio and succinctly diagnosed one of his team’s problems.

“We gotta have more leadership than that,” Riley said.

He was describing a technical foul that went against the Cougars, who proceeded to lose all momentum, winding up with a narrow loss to High Point and opening their season with two straight losses. In the aftermath of that one, it became clear that to turn things around, WSU would need to improve at responding to adversity.

After Washington State’s latest outing, a 72-71 road loss to Duquesne on Tuesday evening, it appears that much is still a work in progress. After leading for nearly 90% of game, the Cougs gave up the lead in the final seconds on an and-one, and on the other end, they couldn’t win the game as guard Lazerek Houston’s floater missed.

“It’s frustrating because there is a clear progression with our team,” said Riley, whose team allowed Duquesne to shoot 52% from the field in the second half. “We are getting better, but this is unacceptable for us to be losing these kinds of games where we control the whole game.”

WSU, which has now started a season with three straight losses for the first time since 1964, will regret this one in large part because of how much it controlled the game. The Cougs led for a total of 34 minutes, 38 seconds, leading by as many as 11. After retaking the lead midway through the first half on a 3-pointer from Tyler Kropp, who scored 10 points to get on the board for the first time all season, the Cougars didn’t lose the lead again until the final sequence.

That went like this: With about 30 seconds left, the Cougs got an acrobatic finish in traffic from guard Sebastian Akins, who totaled nine points. On the other end, Duquesne forward Kerem Konan drove at WSU freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe, who tried to draw a charge. He was called for a block. Konan completed the and-one at the free-throw line, pushing the Dukes ahead 72-71 with 12 seconds left.

But at that point, Duquesne had only been called for four team fouls in the second half, meaning they had two to give before WSU reached the bonus. So when the Cougars got the ball back, by the time the Dukes had committed two fouls, the visitors only had about five seconds to work with. Out of a timeout, WSU got the ball to Houston, who made a move into the paint but couldn’t finish a tough running floater, drifting to the side.

It was a winnable game for WSU, which had three double-digit scorers: Redshirt freshman wing Jaylen Harrell scored 19 points, Houston tallied 12 and Kropp registered 10. But many of the Cougars’ problems in this loss had more to do with two other categories: fouling and rebounds.

In the second half, WSU was whistled for 14 fouls. That resulted in a deluge of free throws for Duquesne, which converted 15 of 19 chances. Also in the second half, the Cougars gave up seven offensive rebounds, which turned into 11 second-chance points for the Dukes.

Another trend went Duquesne’s way in the second period. WSU lost only five turnovers in the first half, doing well to veer away from one of the most consistent problems the Cougars have faced in Riley’s tenure, which is now in its third year. But in the second stanza, the Cougs coughed it up nine times, leading to 14 points off turnovers.

“That second half, we got away from playing our identity, and I think it’s really obvious when you look at the stats,” Riley said in a postgame radio interview. “They had 40 points in the paint, and we had nine turnovers in the second half. Those two things are gonna kill you every time, especially on the road. We let those turnovers lead to transition points.”

Also complicating things for WSU was an injury to transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who missed the first two games of the season with a turned ankle he suffered hours before his team’s season opener last week. He made his season debut on Tuesday, starting and playing 22 minutes, but his outing was cut short with about 3½ minutes to play, when he appeared to injure his ankle again.

It was a costly blow for the Cougs, who had gotten six points and five rebounds from Harrison, a do-it-all wing whose athleticism makes a difference on the glass and on defense. When Harrison went down, WSU subbed in transfer big man Ladji Dembele, who has put up these numbers in three games: seven points on 3-for-12 shooting, including 1-for-6 from deep, 11 rebounds, 10 fouls, five turnovers, one block and two steals.

On the year, WSU is now allowing opponents an effective field -goal percentage of 63%, which ranks No. 347 out of 362 Division I teams. The Cougars are also permitting a 2-point shooting percentage of 65%, which is No. 336. Their defensive problems have surfaced most in the second halves. Here are their opponents’ shooting percentages in the second period this season.

• Davidson: 63%

• High Point: 68%

• Duquesne: 52%

Can the Cougars turn that around? They’ll have a chance to earn their first win this weekend, hosting Division II Northwest at 10 a.m. Saturday. After that, they face a neutral-site game against Hawaii, which will provide an opportunity for these Cougars to prove that Riley is right – that they are progressing.

“We’re figuring out who we can trust out there,” Riley said, “and absolutely, we gotta start shorting that (rotation) a little bit too.”Greg Woods can be reached at 509-459-5587 or at gregw@spokesman.com.
